blocks.x: I want to ask you, Roy, you said that when you were a young man in New Orleans, you heard Tony down there on at least one occasion. I see, remember you were saying that? Heard Tony Jackson in New Orleans?
Oh yes, I heard, that's where I did hear him, was in New Orleans. The reason I heard him in Chicago on one occasion, that's where the one occasion comes in.
What kind of occasion?

Let me try that again. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Boy, you might as well listen to that when you're gone. Thank you. Thank you. How are you going? What is that? That is a song. What? How soon you're all forgotten, and I'll come. She said, oh, I'd better start that again. I'll start the whole thing. I'll start the whole thing. How dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear I think I remember. See, I'm not much good at this one. Which one is this? This is Every Little Bit Helps. It's a song, it's one of the first things I ever heard him play, but I remember now just a little difference in the one major here that he used. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Couldn't have been a stop time piece that I played at that. Might have been. It really wasn't Tony's, but... I don't know if I can play that or not. Oh, I forgot the poetry, please. It's funny. . . Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
Well there must be a number one, do you know that one?

I used to play part of that. It's heavier than the other, in a way it's heavier, there's more octaves in it. I, in the first three, I got pretty familiar with. Number four was a monstrosity. He had chords like that in a terrible... Guy Waterman has the whole series over there by himself right now. And Jerry, you're all set, he wasn't a bit good looking. He sang and played. Sang and played, oh he's wonderful. He'll sit there.
Listen, Jerry plays, sings like him, he sings high pitched.

There's a couple of spots when Jerry recorded that, the homers in a southern town, I don't know if you ever heard of him recording, but there are a couple of spots there that he reminded me of jazz, a little bit like Tony. It's one of my favorite Jerry Roll records. Is it? Yeah, he reminds me a little. It's a wonder he didn't get to singing more earlier. How did, how did you ever get to going down in the district to hear those guys playing? Well, it just, just like I told you, that one night I was just, they had a strong name listening around and I didn't really know where I was. Yeah, New Orleans. Yeah, and I walked there and I heard Tony playing in this, this house there, see. Then I discovered that if I had to stroll around, I could hear him occasionally, I'd again stroll around. I heard Zellie too. Where'd you hear Zellie? Well, I'm pretty sure I heard him at Hilma Burke's one night as I was passing by. It was a summer night and they had all the windows open then. I never had any, I don't know how the house was built or arranged, you know, but evidently the piano was, or the parlor was a couple of rooms back. And I never had heard any music coming out of there before, but this night the, the windows must have been all open and out this music was coming and he, and someone was playing music that, on the type of the Crave and, and, uh, Creepy Feeling. Well he was playing that stuff then, wasn't he? Apparently he was, yeah. Those were in 1910 or earlier? Well, it probably was a little earlier than that, you see, because Zellie picked up on the left, I imagine, by 10, he had really gone. He was there in 1907 and 8, though.
Well then the New Orleans Blues was written in 1906, wasn't it? Well he, yes.

So that's, that sort of thing, sort of Spanish effect there. Well that had some too, but, uh, they, that is a, is a twelve bar piece, and, uh, these, these, uh, these strikes me weren't, you see, the Creepy Feeling and the Crave are, are twelve major pieces, the regular Spanish, like, the, uh, New Orleans Blues, which is a Spanish bass and all, is a, is a twelve bar. Is that where you first met, in general? No, I never knew him there, but I, I know I heard him play.
You didn't actually meet him until Washington, I guess?
No, not until 1938, uh, the spring, before, before he made the library recordings, but.
Did you go down there very often, to his place?

Uh, well, no, not really often, and, uh, still I did go a fair number of times, you know, because after, after a couple of months we got started in trying to get these pieces out for him, you know, those four, four first songs. If you knew, and so. Yeah, no, and, uh, we were working on those, I, I wrote the words to two of them, you know, and tried to, you know, you nominated me, right over there. This is Tony. No, no, it's a general.
Tony Earne. Oh, which one of the two that you wrote the words for? If you knew, and why? That's right, if you knew.

And I wrote the verse to Sweet Substitute, but I didn't claim it, I think I should claim it. I think he should claim it. Oh, yeah. It's a good one. He would, uh, yeah, it's getting a little popularity. Mm-hmm. But, uh, funny, funny thing about it, I say he, he nominated me, I said, well, I said, get Sidney Martin, I said, the, the first thing started on those songs was, uh, was a tune that he wrote for a clarinet player that he wanted to record with. Here? Yes. I don't know that played in an orchestra, and I don't know whose orchestra it was there, but he got in the... You know his name if you heard it. No, I wouldn't know his name, but I think it was, uh, Bill Strickland's orchestra, if you know that name. This is a colored orchestra? No, I think he was right.
A white orchestra.
I think he was right, yeah.

Did you ever know a person who played with him here in Washington named John W. Dews? No. I encountered this man one night, he was driving a taxi cab, and we got to talk about Jolly Roll, he picked us up over there near where the jungle in was. Oh, yeah. And he said, you know, do you know about Jolly Roll? And I said, well, sure. I said, well, I used to play with him. Is that right? And he played with him apparently a lot. Was it clarinet? He played the reeds, he said.

Well, maybe he was a man, but whoever it was disappointed him. He wrote a tune, and, uh, one night, one night or one afternoon, I tried to get around there when the place wasn't busy, so I wouldn't be interfering with anything. I got around there one afternoon, and he played this thing through, what it was, and I said, well, what's that? He said, a little piece I composed. Composed for a clarinet player, and he was going to meet me down at the United Recording Company down there, and he says he never showed up. And he said, that's the piece. I said, well, that's a nice tune. I said, well, that's a nice tune. Which was that? I said, why? Why? I said, what's the name of it? He said, I called it Y. I said, well, why? He said, no reason. He said, it's just, uh, I think that fits the tune. And I said, well, I said, it's a nice tune. I said, why don't you get words put to it? I said, well, you write words put to it. I'm no writer. I said, what? He said, yeah, you can write words put to it. Go ahead. I said, no. I said, get Martin. Get Sidney Martin. You know, Martin was coming around, and he was sort of a newspaper writer, or a article writer, or something. He said, no, never mind, Martin. He said, here. He wrote it unhanded to me. He says, you write words to it. Well, I cracked my skull. And I finally got words to the chorus. It was just the chorus that he had, I know. I got words to the chorus. I took them down to him, handed it to him. I suppose two or three days later, I passed by again. He said, here, take this. I said, what's that? He said, that's a verse for a while. Write words to that. Write words to that. So I had some more words to do. What were the names of those first couple of pieces you did before I started writing these down here? The earlier stuff you did. you did. Well, that, uh... You want to put this?
I think it's often just about the business that he did at Tony Jackson's that he heard Tony do in New Orleans, and then Tony did again in Chicago when he saw him there.

That part comes into a piece I call Recreation Rag. I wrote number two also. I used a little of what I thought was a honky-tonk string in that two bars that turns out to be part of Tiger Rag. Let's see if I can do it without stumbling. . . They whistled that all around town down there. And I don't know if they whistled any more than that, but that got stuck in my head. What was the name of that one? Well, I put it, as I say, into a rag and call it a recreation rag. But this little bar... When did you write that? That's part of the Tiger. I wrote that about 1916. Really? Or 17, yeah. I didn't put it on paper. Well, I put that on paper and sent it the same to us. John Stark sent it back. He says, this is the kind of stuff we like to put out. He says, but the local boys are just on our necks. He says they were standing on one foot waiting for their stuff to come out. So he didn't take it. Do you think you could assimilate Tony on the naked dance? That was his? No, it's any more than that sample I gave, you see.
That's, yeah, that's what it was that he was doing.

That was the, that was the, what gave Jelly the other, let Jelly know what I meant. He probably was playing a variation of it of his own. And, uh, went ahead and then he added a couple of parts when he did it for General Neckler record.

The, uh, you know, is there, I seem to have the idea that Johnny, the Jelly Roll wrote Someday Sweetheart. I mean, well, he said he did. He, well, in the, in the, in the, in the Library of Congress records, he says that, uh, something about Someday Sweetheart. He said the Spikesbugs wrote it anywhere that, with their names on it, so they must have written it. Finally. But somewhere else, somebody said that Jelly Roll, or maybe Jelly does himself.

I, I think he said that, uh, that he had it, and they took it and made a song out of it or something like that, and he said, well, I'm having it. Well, there were two other tunes, you know. But when they, when they began to work on Wolverine Blues, then he said something had to be done.

Uh-huh. Well, there were two other tunes, you know, there was, uh, Some Rainy Day and Maybe Someday. Oh, is that so? Maybe Someday was recorded by Ori's Pods of Pepper, and Some Rainy Day was recorded by Noon. Oh, that's right. And they're very much like, uh, Someday Sweetheart, both tunes. In fact, Some Rainy Day and Maybe Someday are identical. That's right.
Well, uh, does it give, uh, credit to the composer?
Spice Brothers. Spice Brothers. Spice Brothers, yeah. I wondered whether, uh, whether Jelly wrote both variations of the thing. He probably did, if they were very similar.

Well, he, uh, he wrote Frogger. He wrote Froggy Moore. Then he went out west, uh, uh, at least he was in Los Angeles, and, uh, he played it for Spice Brothers, and got hooked up with them, and they, they took part one and part three and wrote, uh, Froggy Moore. Mm-hmm. See? Just used those two parts. Mm-hmm. Then they all came to Chicago and, uh, uh, assigned Froggy Moore to Melrose, and Melrose took the, the second part, the chorus, and wrote, uh, Sweetheart O' Mine. Sweetheart O' Mine. Now I'm having a heck of a time because he claims, Melrose is claiming, because they've got Sweetheart O' Mine, which has that one part that they own the whole thing, uh, Froggy Moore, which has three parts, and which they never owned any part of them. Well, except through, through this devious method of getting it from, uh, Spike Brothers. What does that title mean? Well, you know what Harrison Smith said, that, Froggy Moore, he gives the definition of Froggy, uh, the interpretation of Froggy Moore. He was a vaudeville, uh, contortionist. Mm-hmm. Frogman, Froggy Moore, a frogman, and he went through his contorsions. But I don't think so, I think, Telly was kidding somebody.
Sounds like he might have been kidding Freddie Moore. Well, he might have been. Because, who pops, he's ever seen Freddie Moore play, or he plays, his eyes pop, buddy.

Well, that's, that's my impression that somebody, somebody that had poppy eyes. Oh, he's not going to be good for Freddie Moore. See, because, because Jelly Roll wasn't ignorant, he could, he could write, if he meant Froggy, Froggy Moore, he could have written it. Froggy, but instead of that he wrote F-R-O-G hyphen the I, then he put an I and then M-O-R-E. Well, of course he didn't, that wasn't him to blow, or you know. But that's, that's been my feeling about it.
I don't know whether Freddie Moore was around at that time, it was a little bit later, he played with Oliver, recorded with Oliver. Did he?

Well, Johnny could have met him then. But he certainly did. He wrote that in 1918, Johnny did the original. Oh, did he? That's a little bit of Freddie Moore. Yeah. But, anyhow, it's a funny thing now, there's some park or something in England by the name of Frogmore. Oh, really? Yes, F-R-O-G-M-O-R-E, I ran across that. I started to write a little squib about that, say the telly room was honoring the Queen, Queen Victoria, I don't know, it couldn't have been Queen Victoria, it was too late for her.
Did you get in, when you were in New Orleans, did you get into any of those dance halls down there? Well, I used to look in on them.

I never, I kind of went out to be strolling around, of course they were playing good jazz there in those places. They were pretty rough places, weren't they? Well, they were, they were, well, there was a pretty heavy crowd, you may say, the roughnecks that did that. But I don't recall any disturbance except when they killed Billy Phillips. And that was rough that night. That's Billy Phillips. Yeah, he ran the 101 Ranch. The competition was right across the street at the tuxedo competition. And the story was then, as they tried to develop it, that somebody had hired Chip the Blood and Lefty Louie to come down from New Orleans and bump Billy Phillips off, which he did. And they, but they never caught him and they never hung in on him. It wasn't a few days that both dance halls were still going, were going again. The, the state or the areas that Billy Phillips kept on having the dance hall running. Well, I used to pass by and I'd take a look in there and see what was going on. They, they were, as I say, there was never any rough stuff. There was a very heavy, rough crowd all right, rough necks. And I don't know that they ever had any other activities there. The girls there to dance with the fellas. They danced and they, they got into buying drinks, which is no, a gang of course. But I don't think they had any other activities at that time. They stayed strictly in the dance hall. There's nothing, no connection with any other place that I knew of. And, as I say, there was, I don't recall any other writhing or rough stuff of that time, except when they killed Billy Phillips. But there were three of them that played regularly. And that, that was the only, there was the two, the Tuxedo and the 101 Ranch, and then a place on the next corner back, because as near as I can figure, was Eddie Grosselles. Eddie Grosselles. And that was, that was built for, for that purpose. It was built in the dance hall, and I think King Oliver played in there. I'm very sure he did, because it was the only one. And I was passing by there one night, and there was, the band was playing a very hot piece. And they were just finishing up. And I, I said, well, I want to know what that is. And they were just finishing dancing. And I walked in, I walked the full length of the dance hall, and went my way through the dance, and right back to the player's platform. And King Oliver, I'm sure, was standing up in front there. He just got tootin' tootin' his trumpet. And I said, what's the name of that tune you just played? And he said, that's Chicken Reel. It's a stop-time piece too, you know. They blast out on that . Whatever. It goes on and strong there, Chicken Reel. It was taken from an old folk song. The verse . Well, you know, Doc Sushan said that King Oliver didn't want anybody to know what he was playing. he was playing and when he was a kid, he was a kid with these other boys, he would ask Joe what he was playing and he would always answer the name of the tune, who shot John? Same tune. I guess the present day writers of jazz information and so forth, I think it's funny that I didn't go up and ask who was playing, but I never did. I said, what is that? Tony Jackson was the only one that I made an effort to find out who he was and who in the world was that? I told Hulseiser, I think it was, Hulseiser wrote me and said, do you think that so and so played so and so and so? I wrote him and I said, I never concerned myself as who was playing. For instance, I'd be on the street and alone come a pretty nice... ...curt to me to run out there and ask the bass drummer what his name was. You mean marching band? Yeah, marching band. I said I was enjoying music as far as chasing him up to find out who was playing the bass drum or anything else. Were these usually parades or... No, it could be anything. It's remarkable now. I know before 1910, before 1909, I knew that the music was somehow different. I remember standing on Canal Street one night near Royal. Royal Street was the street where General said that the bar rooms opened up and threw away the keys. They kept going right through it. There was always life down Royal Street. Purely in the bar room sense, you know. Billiard Hall, too, and something like that. But anyhow, I was standing on Canal Street right close to Royal. I couldn't look down. I was close enough so that I could hear it all of a sudden. A nice, pretty, pretty raucous and good, in that sense. Good jazz group coming up there. I thought, boy, this is pretty good. I see what this is. So I stood there waiting for them to come out of Royal Street. And here came about four guys. Yeah. One with a tuba, one with a trumpet. Another with something else. And they were making all kinds of music, you know. Jim and the Prince was it. And it was surprising me. I had a laugh. But it was good. Did you see any ride on the wagon? Huh? Did you see any band ride on the wagon? Well, they used to do that more on the Mardi Gras time or something like that. You know, they'd get out and drag them around town because they'd kill themselves trying to walk all day. They would get in wagons then. And to be around town, of course, now on picnics, they would take the band out and they'd be in the wagon while they were on a picnic. And in 1910, we had a salesman at the Remington Company by the name of Carroll. He was so good that the company promoted him to be manager in Cincinnati. So he went up there for a couple of years, but he didn't like Cincinnati after New Orleans. He'd rather be back in New Orleans. I think he was a native New Orleans man. So by 1911 sometime, he was back in New Orleans. And he brought back a friend from Cincinnati down in New Orleans. And they were working with the Remington Company. And we were on Gravier Street right then, just off of Barone. And one Saturday afternoon, I was working on the books. And up Barone Street comes a good-sized, real legitimate band. Oh, they've been playing hot stuff, you know, coming up. And Carroll stood up immediately. He walked to that front door and stepped out on the walk and watched them go by. And he stepped back in and he said to his friend from Cincinnati, he says, that's music you won't hear anywhere else in the United States. That was no later than 1912, very late, because after that I wasn't a bookkeeper. I went on the road myself then. But he was wise to that. He hadn't heard any of that in Cincinnati. And I know in 1909, which was probably the year I stopped off in Chicago, and I was on the way to visit relatives in Michigan, Grand Rapids. And in Grand Rapids while I was there, the Scotty Band, which was a famous band, I guess they were from Scotland, they'd been playing in Canada and they came through Grand Rapids and they gave a little parade one day and stopped in Campaw Square in the center of the town and played. I happened to be downtown at the time with my niece. We stood there and watched and listened to them playing two or three numbers. I said, well, it's his. Their outfits in New Orleans have got six or eight pieces, can make more of a show than they can. So, people took it for granted, you know. They weren't worrying about, of course, if they had friends playing, whether they got to, you know, the way they got acquainted with the people that played, they'd say, well, five players, and so on.
Plus the musicians all remember who played, but nobody else does down there from that period, I guess.
Well, the friends of the players knew, even the players themselves, they played with these people and all that.
I never remember seeing anything or hearing anything of Black Benny at that time. He was supposed to be a fairly well-known character.

I heard his name, but I think it was according to Saints. I don't remember. But there were players playing places that I would stand on the sidewalk and listen to me and never had an idea who was playing inside. Oh, boy. Jolly, Jolly was not like a lot of people imagine. As far as I was concerned, he didn't do much bragging with me. He would state what he thought, you know. Yeah, well, that's, I remember, as the not bragging. But he depended, I think, in my case, I think he depended on the fact that he knew I lived in New Orleans, and I knew a lot of that stuff myself, you know.

Well, I used to talk to him, and then, because I asked him about a lot of other musicians and all that, you know. He never talked much about himself, but he had plenty to say about Umber Simeon, for example, and Freddie Kepler and Perez. Yeah, that's right. He liked them.

Yeah, he liked them. And the funny thing about that, see, I had, I'd been pretty much out of Bud Rack time and enough. To about 1925, I'd bought a few records now and then, most with piano records. But in 1925, I started going to night school, and I was working daytime, and I didn't have time for anything else. So I dropped out of my life entirely, almost, to music. I didn't play much. My nephew came low, he was playing, and I wouldn't pay much attention. So, I started to tell something I'm going to forget. What would you show that I was going to tell? Oh, after I met Jenny, I began to look up these different jazz players, you know, and I'd inquire about them now and then. So I asked him about the big speederback. I replied to the back, I said, did you? How much power goes to build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build build

I asked him about Begg Speederbeck. I said, are you familiar with him? He said, yes. I said, have you heard him play? He said, yes, I heard him play. I said, well, was he good? He said, yes, he was good. He wasn't as good as they say he was. That's about his course. He said, no, I've never heard him play. He said, yes, he was good. He said, he wasn't as good as they say.

I was close at the time. I was 38 and was here. I was 20 years old. I was asking him about Frank Teschmaker and all these people. They were all right, but he said, these boys like Jimmy Noon and Umar Simeon. It was so much better. There was no comparison. It's true, of course.

He said, well, he wasn't diplomatic. He knew the true stand for guff, you know. Then there were some, of course, that would needle him. They'd start in, you know. Sorry about it. I think it was Hotlips Page one time. I don't know whether he was needleing him or not, but he meant Hotlips Page. He asked him what he was doing or something like that. And he said, Page replied, says, one of them says, I'm playing Kansas City Jazz now. General Rowe says, Kansas City Jazz.
I didn't know such thing. He said, I'm the man that carried that. He carried that into Kansas City.

Kansas City Jazz. I don't know whether you read it or not. I wrote that first little thing I wrote for the record changer was just a little paragraph about Johnny being in New York. And he went to a nightclub where a couple of boogie woogie players were the star attraction. I guess they were the only thing there. And they were playing the boogie woogie stuff. And Johnny got persuaded to give a few examples of his stuff. You know, he played and went over all right. And he was telling Lomax about playing there, you know. And Johnny says, well, he says, did you do all right? Johnny says, yes, I did all right. He says, did you do all right? He says, do all right in comparison to those boogie players? Johnny says, sure, I did all right with those boogie players. And Lomax coming up, he says, did you? Did you do as well or do as good as those boogie woogie players? He said, why shouldn't I do as good as guys that only know one, too? It was true.
Why shouldn't he tell the term of that? He's probably talking about Ammons and Johnson.

It might have been Ammons and Johnson, or Johnson and Turner. Who was it? There's a couple of them that were playing around New York. Yeah, they were around. Anyhow, the guys that only know one, too. That's what got it with Handy, too, you know. Because Handy hadn't really done something with it. The blues made plenty of money out of it. Johnny said, blues wasn't considered music in those days, which was a fact. They'd hush you up as you started playing it down there and go on and that kind of thing. And also, I think it was Mudd Carey, they quote him as saying blues, and they said only the ignorant played blues. But when Handy showed you could make some money out of it, then everybody began to get it through. And it certainly did spread it.
You hear about the Bolden band playing ragtime. I wonder what they mean by that.
Well, my belief is that the first jazz bands were really ragtime bands.
They play ragtime as ragtime as thought of by Joplin and those people.

Well, no, I don't think so. The New Orleans ragtime was a little different from most of it that was played in the published ones that I could form an opinion of. I think the New Orleans ragtime lends itself a little better to jazz than the St. Louis ragtime. Now, you take the Maple Leaf, the Maple Leaf is so complete, you may say, such a tightly knit thing, that when you want to really vary it, you've got to do something like Jelly did. He altered that thing completely, you may say. Well, it became a jolly old composition. Yeah, he says that was the way I played it. He said, I think, he says, well, it has to be a bad jazz.
Well, it has to be a bad jazz. It was the same thing with the original rag, of course, too.

Yeah, yeah. Well, he told me afterwards, I guess I complimented him, I said, that's very fine. He says, oh, he says, if the boys had let me, he says, I'd really tore that thing up. He says, but they held me down. Really? With the original rag? Yeah, rich and rich. He says, I was really going to do something that piece, he said, but they held it down.
You mean, you mean, you mean, you know, part of it?
Charles Edward Smith, I suppose it was.

Yeah, that's right, Charles. That's right. Well, he also, I talked to him, the last time I saw him was in New York, and he played the test pressings of those things just before they were issued. And he said that he didn't like the way he did Michigan Water. They insisted he do it that way, and he didn't want to do it that way. And I don't know what he had in mind.

Well, I'll say this about Michigan Water. Clarence Williams had published, claimed it, in 1923 about. Whereas, according to John Lewis, Tony was playing that thing years before that. And as far as the tune itself goes, the verse, I had heard it before that thing, considerably. And I think maybe they got the music of Clarence Williams, and had him follow that to a certain extent, because in a way he does follow, not too closely. But Clarence Williams doubtless picked it up from Tony or from somebody else around there. I never heard Tony play it, but I had heard it around the morning, Michigan Water Blues, after that. They used to say Michigan Water tastes like sherry wine, but the Mississippi Water tastes like turpentine. That was the first person I heard of him. He used to kid about or laugh about Clarence. He said, no, it was, I'll say his name. It was Fats Waller. He says, Fats, he says, he's interested to see a little bit of something here he likes, a little bit of something there he likes, a little bit of something somewhere else he likes. He puts them all together, you've got a Fats Waller piece. He said, but anyway, with Clarence Williams, he grabbed a hole. He grabbed a hole. He's a little bit of a hole.

Well, you know, I think that the much more talented composer than Clarence was the... Oh, that other one. Spencer. Spencer, yeah. Yeah, he was. Spencer was a beautiful thing. Well, Spencer was a pretty well-known piano player in New Orleans too, wasn't he?
I don't know.
I believe he was, and yet he never recorded.

Never recorded, no. Well, now I heard something different from that, to the truth, there's something that... late... No, no, no, no. A fellow from Indiana, Joe Russell Robinson. He commented on a tune that, St. Thomas Spencer's tunes that was played to some singer. He said, if you're listening to hear Williams play on that, he didn't, or he couldn't. He said, I'm the man that played to come in for that. That was Russell Roberts. I don't know anything further than that. It's Spencer Williams. Spencer, yeah. Spencer Williams. So I don't know. You hear lots of tales about it. They say that Joplin wasn't a very good player. He's not, not compared to the other boys. But I heard a party that lived in Memphis, I think it was Memphis, that told me that if they could get Scott Joplin for their parties to do the play, they didn't want anything else. He offered that remark off hand.
Well, don't you think this is probably Joplin on these roles that like this... I'm pretty sure they do. I mean, the label says just one thing. It says the title in Scott Joplin, and that's all.
I have a pretty strong feeling also I've heard of that role by the Maple Leaf. I think he played that too. I heard that.
It sure sounds like, I don't know who else it could be who would play that way, you know.
Well, he follows the music group much on this than the gladioles. That's what he's making at all. No, that's just what I wish.
Do you have any more piano left on you tonight, Roy?
Well, I don't know. I don't know if it's very good. I'm not up to par. I don't know. Let's see. Let's see. Let's see. Let's see. The End The End The End The End
The End The End The End The End
The End The End The End

segments.title: Hearing Tony Jackson in New Orleans and Chicago
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about hearing Tony Jackson; Carew says he heard him in New Orleans and once in Chicago.

segments.title: Garbled piano playing and talk of a piece series
segments.summary: Carew restarts a piece at the piano (transcript garbled); they discuss a numbered series of pieces and a singer-pianist.

segments.title: Jelly Roll's singing and Carew hearing Tony and Jelly Roll in New Orleans' district
segments.summary: Carew compares Jelly Roll's singing to Tony Jackson, recalls strolling the district and hearing Tony and Jelly Roll play, and the Spanish tinge in Crave and New Orleans Blues.

segments.title: Meeting Jelly Roll in Washington and writing words to his songs
segments.summary: Carew first met Morton in 1938 before the library recordings, visited his place, wrote words to two songs including Sweet Substitute, and a taxi driver claims to have played with Morton.

segments.title: Morton's tune for a clarinetist and the title 'Why'
segments.summary: Morton plays a tune he composed for a clarinet player who never showed at the recording company; Carew writes words for the chorus.

segments.title: Recreation Rag and the Tiger Rag strain
segments.summary: Carew describes his own Recreation Rag, written about 1916-17, using a strain heard in New Orleans that is part of Tiger Rag, and how Morton recorded a variation.

segments.title: Who wrote Someday Sweetheart
segments.summary: They discuss Morton's claim on Someday Sweetheart and the similar tunes Some Rainy Day and Maybe Someday.

segments.title: Froggy Moore, Spikes Brothers and the title's meaning
segments.summary: Carew explains how Morton's Froggy Moore was split and republished, and debates whether the title refers to a contortionist or Freddie Moore.

segments.title: New Orleans dance halls and the killing of Billy Phillips
segments.summary: Carew recalls looking into rough dance halls and the murder of Billy Phillips, who ran the 101 Ranch.

segments.title: Black Benny and what Morton said of other musicians
segments.summary: Discussion of Black Benny, Morton not bragging with Carew, and his praise of Simeon, Keppard and Perez.

segments.title: Carew's years away from jazz and Morton on Bix and Hot Lips Page
segments.summary: After meeting Morton Carew asked about jazz players; Morton's opinion of Bix Beiderbecke and the Chicago players, and his exchange with Hot Lips Page about Kansas City jazz.

segments.title: Morton on boogie-woogie players and on Handy and the blues
segments.summary: Morton's remark about boogie pianists who only know one trick, and his view that blues was disreputable until Handy made money from it.

segments.title: Ragtime and early jazz: Bolden, Maple Leaf and Morton's treatment
segments.summary: Carew argues early jazz bands played New Orleans ragtime that suited jazz better than St. Louis ragtime; Morton on altering Maple Leaf and being held down on a record.

segments.title: Michigan Water Blues, Clarence Williams, Spencer Williams and Fats Waller
segments.summary: Disputed authorship of Michigan Water Blues, comments on Fats Waller and Clarence Williams, and talk of Spencer Williams.

segments.title: Scott Joplin's playing and piano rolls
segments.summary: Carew relays opinions of Joplin's playing and they discuss rolls labeled as Joplin.

segments.title: Closing of the tape
segments.summary: Interviewer asks Carew for more piano; he demurs and the tape ends.
